title: Building Social World Model with Large Language Models
one_liner: Model how public beliefs change after events by learning state transitions from time-stamped social signals.
lead: People do not hold fixed beliefs about elections, policy, or markets. Their beliefs shift after debates, court rulings, scandals, and new evidence. This paper asks whether a language-model-based system can learn those shifts as a world model for social belief change. The goal is not only to predict the next belief state, but also to describe why the change happened in terms of event-driven state transitions.

problem.h2: Why social belief forecasting is hard
paras: Forecasting a physical process is easier when the hidden state has direct measurements. Social belief is different because what people think is only partly visible. We may observe prices in prediction markets, headlines, and event times, but the underlying belief state must be inferred indirectly.

That makes social forecasting hard in two ways. The system must estimate the current belief state from partial evidence, and it must learn how major events move that state over time. The paper builds a Social World Model to handle both pieces together.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Treat collective belief as a hidden state that changes after events, then learn the transition from observed time-stamped social data.

panels.title: 1. Start with a belief state
panels.caption: The current public belief is hidden but leaves clues in observed signals.

panels.title: 2. A new event happens

panels.caption: Events create pressure that can move the belief state.

panels.caption: Observed market changes and related text give partial evidence about the shift.

panels.title: 4. Update the state

panels.caption: The model learns how events tend to move beliefs over time.

panels.title: 5. Predict the next step
panels.caption: A learned transition rule supports forecasting and interpretation.

steps.text: Collect time-stamped data such as market probabilities and aligned event information.
Use observed signals to infer the current social belief state at each time.
Model how new events change the hidden state from one time step to the next.
Roll the transition rule forward to predict later states.
Check whether predicted belief movement matches real shifts in the benchmark.

paras: The paper changes the target of prediction. Instead of forecasting observed prices directly, it inserts a hidden belief state and learns how events push that state from one step to the next.
object.object: Hidden social belief state over time

hidden.name: Current collective belief state
paras: This hidden state is the paper's core quantity. It stands for what the crowd currently believes before the next event arrives, even though that belief cannot be read off perfectly from any single observed signal.
The model infers the hidden state from noisy observations and then updates it after each event. That matters because price movements are often only a surface trace of deeper belief change.

heat.caption: Darker means the belief state is harder to estimate or more likely to shift sharply.

reads.html: The model is trying to track what the crowd currently believes, not just what the latest price happens to be.
Observed social signals are treated as indirect evidence about a hidden belief state, meaning a state that is not observed directly, and that state evolves through event-driven transitions.

paras: Adding a hidden belief state helps because it separates observation noise from belief dynamics. A price can move for several short-term reasons, but the underlying belief update may be smoother or more interpretable. By estimating the hidden state first, the model can learn a clearer transition rule for how events change beliefs.

Event conditioning matters because not all time steps are alike. A routine day and a debate night should not produce the same update behavior. The model performs better when the transition is tied to the event context, because that context explains why one observation sequence should lead to a sharp shift while another should barely move the belief state.

stages.s: infer the current hidden belief state
update that state using the current event

math.words: The next belief state comes from the current belief state plus the effect of the current event, and observations are generated from that updated state.
symbols: the hidden collective belief state at time t
the event information available at time t, such as a debate or policy announcement
the learned update rule that maps the current belief state and event into the next belief state
the belief state after the event-driven update
the visible signal at time t, such as a market probability or related social measurement
the mapping from hidden belief state to observed signal

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the current market suggests a candidate win chance near 0.54, so belief_t is centered around 54%.
A strong debate performance occurs at time t.
The learned transition says this type of event usually shifts belief upward by 0.08 when the race is close.
The readout step predicts that observed market prices should also rise toward 62%, though not necessarily exactly because prices are noisy.

math.note: The paper trains this hidden-state model from observed sequences rather than from direct labels of belief shifts.

charts.title: Standard time-series forecasters
charts.note: These models track patterns in the observed sequence but explain event-driven belief shifts less clearly.

charts.title: Social World Model
charts.note: Performance improves because the model learns event-conditioned state updates rather than only surface trends.

items.html: A single event can push different groups in different directions, so one shared belief update may miss important structure.
Prediction markets and related social signals can be noisy or thinly traded, so the inferred belief state can drift when the visible signal is unstable.
A forecast can fail when the event record omits background conditions, because the same headline can move beliefs differently in different contexts.
Use dense time-stamped observations, align events carefully, and evaluate both predictive fit and the plausibility of the inferred belief shifts.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small benchmark around one domain such as election markets. Use a sequence of daily market prices and a matching sequence of major events. Then compare a direct next-step forecaster against a simple hidden-state model that updates belief after each event.

The demo should show that the hidden-state model predicts belief swings more accurately around important events because it represents the event-driven transition explicitly instead of treating every day as the same kind of step.
demo.metric_eq: forecast_error = average absolute difference between predicted and observed market value ; event_window_error = same error measured only near major events
demo.closing: If the hidden-state model reduces error around major event windows, it is demonstrating the paper's main advantage.
